title: The Ivy League
summary: Josh and Chuck record in 3D audio week, using binaural ear microphones, and explain the Ivy League. They cover the eight member schools (the "Ancient Eight"), the origin of the name (the Roman numeral IV myth, the Stanley Woodward and 1937 Columbia-Penn story, Alan Gould's 1935 AP usage), and the fact that the league is essentially a Division I FCS athletic conference formed through the 1945 Ivy Group Agreement to control football. They discuss sports rules (no athletic scholarships, no redshirting, limits on grad students), the Ivy League's elite status and alumni representation in government, business, law and the Supreme Court, presidents who attended Ivy schools, endowments totaling about $140 billion (Harvard about $40 billion), and the 2019 college admissions bribery scandal. They also cover the lawsuit over anti-Asian bias in Harvard admissions and Opportunity Insights research on income mobility and access. The episode ends with a listener mail from Emily in Chicago about exclusion of women of color, poor women, and LGBTQ women in second-wave feminism, including Betty Friedan and Rita Mae Brown.

segments.title: 3D audio week opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about recording in 3D audio week with binaural ear microphones, reunite in the same studio after a long break, and read friends' quotes about Ivy League and grad school experiences.

segments.title: What the Ivy League is
segments.summary: The hosts list the eight Ivy schools, known as the Ancient Eight, and note that the Ivy League is essentially an athletic conference. They mention Division I FCS status and sports where the league competes.

segments.title: Origin of the name Ivy League
segments.summary: The hosts debunk the Roman numeral IV story and describe the 1937 Columbia-Penn assignment and Stanley Woodward's supposed coinage. They note Alan Gould's 1935 AP print usage and the ivy-covered buildings.

segments.title: Ivy Group Agreement and sports rules
segments.summary: The Ivy Group Agreement is described as a way to control football's influence and balance it with academics. The hosts cover rules banning athletic scholarships, redshirting, and certain grad student play, and mention notable teams like rowing and skiing.

segments.title: Elitism and alumni power
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the Ivy League's elite status and the five-to-sixfold advantage for top positions. They cite Supreme Court justices, presidents including Obama, both Bushes, and Clinton, and the reputation effect of an Ivy degree. They also mention Ivy Plus schools.

segments.title: Endowments and tax
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the combined endowments of about $140 billion, with Harvard's about $40 billion. They cover investment returns, the 2017 endowment tax, and per-student spending compared with second-tier schools.

segments.title: Admissions scandals and bias lawsuit
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the admissions bribery scandal involving Lori Loughlin and Felicity Huffman, with fake sports recruitment. They also cover the lawsuit alleging anti-Asian bias at Harvard, which Harvard won on appeal, and the role of admissions coaches.

segments.title: Socioeconomic diversity and mobility
segments.summary: The hosts cite Opportunity Insights research showing that children from the top one percent are far more likely to attend an Ivy than those from the bottom twenty percent. They note that Ivies are good at mobility but have low access, and discuss students feeling like outsiders.

segments.title: Listener mail: feminism from Emily in Chicago
segments.summary: Emily from Chicago writes that Betty Friedan's second-wave feminism excluded poor women, women of color, and LGBTQ women, and that Rita Mae Brown was sidelined. Josh and Chuck agree and sign off.
